title: Musicians who left New Orleans and local support
summary: Many players left for the road or California in the 50s and early 60s; New Orleans takes its musicians for granted and local talent needs support.

story.theme_name: Getting paid: wages, tips and leaving over money
story.community_name: Managers, bookers and the business of getting work

blocks.x: You know what, a lot of guys who went on the road, and Earl King would do this to me, I'll be with him and he'll say, see that guy, he's a great saxophone player. Nobody knows what, because he was always, they left. They were always gone. Yeah. So we don't, for the cats who stayed, like Red Tyler, Red didn't go on the road a lot. He was on sessions, but we know him from his records he was on.

Well that's why one of the things I used to say, if we would all leave, we wouldn't have anybody say hello to when we come back. You know what I'm saying? Everybody was leaving in the 50s and early 60s, according to California and other places. And there's a lot of people that, somebody would be talking about musicians, they'd say, well I've never heard of him. They'd say, well he's been here all his life. He played. There's quite a few guys. Harry Nance, the drummer. Been everywhere twice, played with a lot of people. New Orleans we take it for granted. We respect the musicians, but we just take it for granted. Oh I saw him yesterday on the Do Man's trailer. Yeah, I was in the wash of Red with him. And to get the support that the guys need for local talent, and to get the support that the guys need for local talent. It's very hard, you know. Everybody loves a winner after something happened or a guy died. Everybody know him, you know. But I try to get out and support the local talent.
